results.content:
# #4 ➤

## Investing in professional services as a startup

Merge is also investing heavily in professional services, a move that might look wrong if you believe the standard playbook about software margins. But AI has broken that playbook, anyway.

“Services and partnerships will become increasingly more important,” says Shensi. Betting on this, she asked one of her team members to create a new function that combines services and partnerships.

This has also been informed by a significant change in their customer composition. “When we first started, we were mostly selling to startups, but over the past few years, we’ve mostly transitioned to supporting enterprise companies, and they need more support.” [...] There was another interesting emergence they ran into mid-implementation: some enterprises can’t even use AI because they’re stuck on legacy systems with no public APIs. Their data is trapped in systems that predate the cloud.

> “For a lot of companies, they can’t even use AI because they’re currently using on-prem systems or legacy software that doesn’t have a public API and that a lot of vendors are not willing to connect to.”

Merge’s solution here has been to lean heavily into a role that is making waves: Forward-Deployed Engineers. This team builds custom connectors for on-prem and homegrown systems, making sure customers with system or security constraints are still able to deploy AI.

Source: First Round Review [...] # #5 ➤

## Looking ahead

Shensi thinks there’s a lot of opportunity for connectivity in the AI space that no one else is really targeting. “It’s becoming increasingly clear that context is king, especially when it comes to AI, and there’s a ceiling for what reasoning can do without data.”

Merge’s Unified API has helped SaaS companies offer integrations at scale successfully. With Merge Agent Handler, they are helping AI companies connect their agents to systems securely and without any headaches.

That’s them solving integrations, twice.

Shensi is thoroughly excited. “Every SaaS company will eventually become an AI company; so will a lot of non-SaaS companies. Increasingly a lot of buyers are expecting AI in products for personalization and better workflows.”

results.title: The “Merge” With AI Has Already Begun
results.content: complain. Replacing humans with AI in the workplace is yet another step toward a world dominated by artificial entities rather than human beings. [...] This conditioning is further reinforced, in subtle but effective ways, by claims from AI boosters that human beings are fundamentally no different from the large language models (LLMs) that power chatbots like ChatGPT. During an interview last year, Altman complained: “People talk about how much energy it takes to train an AI model… But it also takes a lot of energy to train a human. It takes, like, 20 years of life and all of the food you eat during that time before you get smart.” This view simultaneously anthropomorphizes AI while dehumanizing people. It suggests that we are just biological forms of AI that undergo a “training” process not all that different from LLMs. It implies that we’re distinguished from AI in degree rather than kind. [...] For those of us on Team Human—rather than Team Posthuman—who don’t want digital beings to replace our species, we must be vigilant about the slow creep of AI normalcy. Each small step toward a digital future may appear relatively trivial: “All” AI is doing is writing students’ term papers, providing companionship, assisting people in the workplace, generating songs on Spotify, and so on. To be sure, there are plenty of people upset about these changes. But after initial protestations, many of us become acclimated to the new function of AI in our lives and society.

# Brilliant, Broken, and Frustrating: My Deep Dive into Amazon’s Kiro AI IDE, the Flawed Junior Developer

François Dexemple

We’ve all been there. You throw a few prompts at an AI coding tool, and like magic, a functional app appears. It’s the peak of “vibe coding” — fast, exciting, and instantly gratifying. But then comes the hangover, and, oh boy, I have personally hit this wall hard. The requirements were fuzzy. The design decisions were undocumented. Does the output even solve the problem? What was once a fun prototype quickly becomes a maintenance nightmare; without clear design documentation, future changes are just guesswork. This is why so many AI-built prototypes hit a wall.
